title: Troubleshooting Guide
text:
TipIn this section




Diagnosing convergence problems
Fixing energy drift and NaN values
Resolving performance bottlenecks
Common pitfalls and their solutions





When a simulation fails or produces unexpected results, systematic diagnosis is essential:

Check energy conservation — does TotEng drift? Is PotEng stable?
Check forces — are any atoms experiencing huge forces?
Check charges — are electrode charges oscillating wildly?
Check geometry — are atoms overlapping? Are regions correct?






Electrode charges oscillate wildly between timesteps (e.g., ±10 e on one electrode per step).



Cause
Solution




eta too small
Increase eta (try 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 Å⁻¹)


eta too large
Decrease eta (try 0.5, 0.3 Å⁻¹)


Timestep too large
Reduce dt to 0.5 fs


Overlapping atoms
Run minimization before dynamics


Tolerance too tight
Use kspace_style pppm 1e-4






NaN or Inf appears in PotEng, Temp, or other quantities.



Cause
Solution




Atoms overlapping
Minimize before dynamics; check pair_coeff


Bonds too stretched
Use fix shake to constrain; reduce timestep


Kspace tolerance
Use looser tolerance (1e-4)


Electrode too close
Increase electrode separation


eta too small
Increase eta for better matrix conditioning






ERROR: Fix electrode: matrix inversion failed



Cause
Solution




Singular matrix
Increase eta; check for overlapping atoms


Too many electrode atoms
Use algo mat_cg or algo cg


Geometric issue
Verify electrode geometry is valid






PPPM cannot achieve requested tolerance.



Cause
Solution




Too many close contacts
Minimize; separate overlapping atoms


Box too anisotropic
Adjust kspace parameters


Tolerance too tight
Use 1e-4 instead of 1e-5









Total energy increases or decreases monotonically over time.



Cause
Solution




Timestep too large
Reduce dt (try 0.5 fs, 1 fs)


Cutoff too small
Increase cutoff (12 Å for water)


Thermostat conflict
Remove one thermostat


Force spike
Minimize before running



Check energy conservation:
# Run NVE for 10 ps
fix conservative all nve
run 10000    # 10 ps at 1 fs

# In output, check TotEng drift
# Acceptable: < 0.1% over 10 ps



PotEng goes to large negative or positive values.



Cause
Solution




Atoms too close
Minimize; check pair_coeff (epsilon too large)


Electrode atoms too close to electrolyte
Increase LJ repulsion


Bonds over-stretched
Use fix shake; reduce timestep






Temp is far from target even with thermostat.







Cause
Solution




Damping time wrong
For Langevin, 100.0 is reasonable; try 50.0 or 200.0


Thermostat on frozen atoms
Only thermostat mobile atoms


Initial velocities too hot/cold
Use velocity all create 300.0 12345 before dynamics









# Print atom positions near problematic region
dump debug all custom 1 debug.xyz id type x y z

# Check which atoms are in which group
group bot print

# Check box dimensions
print "Box: $(xhi) $(yhi) $(zhi)"

# Check for overlapping regions
region bot check overlap



Common when creating atoms in overlapping regions.
# Don't do this:
region bot block 0 20 0 20 0 10
create_atoms 1 region bot
region top block 0 20 0 20 0 10    # OVERLAPS with bot
create_atoms 2 region top
Fix: Ensure regions don’t overlap.



# Correct: regions cover full box height with gap for electrolyte
region box block 0 20 0 20 0 60
region bot block 0 20 0 20 0 5
region top block 0 20 0 20 55 60
region elyte block 0 20 0 20 5 55    # Gap between 5 and 55






ERROR: kspace style pppm is not supported with fix electrode
Cause: Standard pppm doesn’t provide electrode interaction matrices.
Fix:
kspace_style pppm/electrode 1e-5    # Electrode-aware version



ERROR: Fix electrode group has no atoms
Cause: Group name doesn’t exist or has no atoms.
Fix:
group bot region bot    # Define group BEFORE fix
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp ...



Electrode potentials are always in volts regardless of units setting.
units metal    # eV, but potential is still in VOLTS, not eV
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805    # -1.0 V, not -1.0 eV






If electrode charges take too long to equilibrate:







Cause
Solution




Matrix too large
Use algo mat_cg instead of mat_inv


Tolerance too tight
Loosen kspace tolerance


Too many electrode atoms
Reduce electrode thickness (3-4 Å sufficient)

title: The ELECTRODE Package
text:
TipIn this section




Three fix styles: electrode/conp, electrode/conq, electrode/thermo
Algorithm choices and when to use each
Kspace compatibility and slab modifications
Output interpretation





The ELECTRODE package implements constant potential, constant charge, and thermopotentiostat methods for electrode-electrolyte simulations. It was developed by Ahrens-Iwers, Tee, and Meissner and first released in LAMMPS 4May2022.
Key capabilities: - Enforce fixed electrostatic potential on electrode groups - Compute induced charges as function of geometry and electrolyte - Track fluctuating potentials in constant charge mode - Model thermal fluctuations (Johnson-Nyquist noise) in electrochemistry
Requirements: - KSPACE package - LAPACK and BLAS (or -D USE_INTERNAL_LINALG=yes with CMake)





cmake -B build -S . \
  -D PKG_ELECTRODE=yes \
  -D PKG_KSPACE=yes \
  -D USE_INTERNAL_LINALG=yes
cmake --build build



Not supported. ELECTRODE requires CMake.






Purpose: Hold the electrostatic potential on each electrode group fixed; charges fluctuate to maintain the constraint.
Physical meaning: Models a potentiostat — the voltage is controlled, charge is the response.
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 couple top 1.0 symm on








Argument
Description
Notes




group
Electrode group to constrain
Must be defined with group command


potential
Electrode potential in volts
Can be variable for dynamic control


eta
Gaussian smearing width (Å⁻¹)
Typical: 1.0–2.0 (real) or 0.2–0.5 (metal)


couple groupName V
Additional electrode at potential V
Can specify multiple couples


symm on/off
Enforce total charge neutrality
Usually on for capacitor-like systems





Any equal-style variable can be used for potential:
variable V equal ramp(-1.0, 1.0)    # sweep from -1 to +1 V over run
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp v_V 1.805 couple top 1.0
variable V equal "2.0 * sin(time * 0.01)"    # oscillating potential
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp v_V 1.805




Purpose: Set the total charge on each electrode group; potentials fluctuate.
Physical meaning: Models a galvanostat — charge injection/extraction is controlled, voltage is the response.
fix fxconq bot electrode/conq -0.5 1.805 couple top 0.5 symm on








Argument
Description
Notes




charge
Total charge on electrode group
In units consistent with units setting


eta
Gaussian smearing width
Same as conp


couple
Additional electrode at charge Q
Not potential



Output: The vector component f_fxconq[2], f_fxconq[3], etc. gives the actual potential on each electrode — can be monitored to compute voltage response.



Purpose: Add thermal fluctuations (Johnson-Nyquist noise) to both potential and charge.
Physical meaning: Models the thermodynamic consistency of charge/potential fluctuations. Essential for fluctuation-dissipation studies and non-equilibrium dynamics.
fix fxthermo bot electrode/thermo -1.0 1.805 300.0 12345 50.0








Argument
Description
Notes




potential
Mean potential
Fluctuates around this


eta
Gaussian smearing
Same as other fixes


temp
Temperature (K)
For thermal noise amplitude


seed
Random seed
Set explicitly for reproducibility


tau_v
Potential relaxation time
Controls how fast potential relaxes



Physical basis: The fluctuation-dissipation theorem relates thermal noise to dissipative properties. For electrochemistry, the thermopotentiostat adds fluctuations to both potential and charge with correct statistics.




The algo keyword controls how the capacitance/elastance problem is solved:



Algorithm
Precomputation
Memory
Speed
Electrode Motion




mat_inv
Capacitance matrix C (N²)
High
Fast
Static only


mat_cg
Elastance matrix S (N²)
Medium
Medium
Static only


cg
None
Low
Slowest
Allowed



Where N = number of electrode groups (not atoms).



Precompute and invert the capacitance matrix at startup
On-the-fly charge calculation: q = C⁻¹ · (V - V0)
Fast for small-to-medium electrode systems
Memory-intensive: stores full N×N matrix
Electrodes must remain fixed (matrix is geometry-specific)

Use when: < 10,000 electrode atoms, static electrodes, need fastest per-step performance




Precompute the elastance matrix (inverse of capacitance)
Use conjugate gradient solver to find charges
Less memory than mat_inv (same matrix size, but CG is iterative)
Slower per step than mat_inv but comparable overall for medium systems

Use when: Medium systems where memory matters; limited electrode motion




No precomputation
Solve full linear system each timestep via conjugate gradient
Slowest per step
Required for moving electrodes (charging/discharging dynamics)

Use when: Electrodes move significantly; very large electrode systems



# Small static system → mat_inv (fastest)
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 algo mat_inv

# Medium static system → mat_cg (balanced)
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 algo mat_cg

# Dynamic electrodes → cg (only option)
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 algo cg






ELECTRODE requires electrode-aware kspace styles that provide: 1. Electrode-electrode interaction matrix 2. Electrode-electrolyte interaction vector



kspace_style ewald/electrode 1e-5
kspace_style pppm/electrode 1e-5
kspace_style pppm/electrode/intel 1e-5    # Intel-optimized
DO NOT use standard ewald or pppm with ELECTRODE — they lack the electrode interaction matrices.



kspace_modify slab 3          # 2D Ewald correction (non-periodic z)
kspace_modify one-step        # faster elastance computation; less accurate
kspace_modify force 1e-4     # override tolerance
slab 3 is standard for non-periodic z geometries. The number 3 refers to the dimension being non-periodic (z).









Option
Description
Values




algo
Solver algorithm
mat_inv, mat_cg, cg


symm
Charge neutrality
on, off


ffield
Finite-field mode
on, off


etypes
Type-based neighbor lists
on, off


couple
Additional electrode group
groupName V_or_Q






fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 couple top 1.0 ffield on symm on

Uses periodic boundary in z
Potential difference applied via internal E-field: E = V / dz
No vacuum region needed; smaller z-dimension possible
Requires symm on (total charge neutrality)

Use when: you want smaller cells; better for some geometries; want infinite stack model



fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 write_inv 1000    # save every 1000 steps
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 read_inv restart.elast    # load at startup
The write_inv saves the elastance matrix. Use read_inv to reload on restart. (Standard LAMMPS restart files don’t yet support ELECTRODE state.)



For real metal response (quantum corrections):
fix_modify fxconp tf 0.001    # Thomas-Fermi screening length
Adds metallic screening beyond the simple dielectric model. Use when electrode is a real metal (Au, Pt, etc.) and quantum effects matter.






f_ID — scalar: the energy added to the system by the fix.
For constant potential: -Σ q_i V_i (work done by electrodes on the system)
Check this for energy conservation (should be small fluctuations around constant in NVE).



f_ID[2], f_ID[3], … — potential on each electrode group.
For electrode/conq: these are the fluctuating potentials (computed response) For electrode/conp: these should match the specified potentials (convergence check)
Access in variable:
variable V_bot equal f_fxconp[2]
variable V_top equal f_fxconp[3]



f_ID[4] through f_ID[4+N] — rows of the capacitance matrix.
For analysis of C_ij structure.




# ============================================
# Constant Potential Electrode-Electrolyte
# ============================================

units metal
atom_style charge
boundary p p f

# --- Box and geometry ---
variable Lx equal 20
variable Ly equal 20
variable Lz equal 60

region box block 0 $Lx 0 $Ly 0 $Lz
create_box 3 box    # 3 atom types: bot, top, electrolyte

region bot block 0 $Lx 0 $Ly 0 5
region top block 0 $Lx 0 $Ly 55 $Lz
region elyte block 0 $Lx 0 $Ly 5 55

create_atoms 1 region bot
create_atoms 2 region top
create_atoms 3 region elyte

group bot region bot
group top region top
group elyte region elyte
group electrode union bot top

# --- Force field ---
pair_style lj/cut/coul/long 10.0

# Electrode-electrode (soft repulsion)
pair_coeff 1 1 0.01 3.0
pair_coeff 2 2 0.01 3.0
pair_coeff 1 2 0.005 3.0

# Electrolyte LJ (SPC/E water + ions)
pair_coeff 3 3 0.155 3.166    # water O
pair_coeff 3 4 0.0 0.0        # water H (if present)
pair_coeff 1 3 0.005 3.1      # bot-water
pair_coeff 2 3 0.005 3.1      # top-water

kspace_style pppm/electrode 1e-5
kspace_modify slab 3

# --- ELECTRODE fix ---
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 couple top 1.0 symm on

# --- Integrators ---
fix frozen all nve           # frozen electrodes
fix mytemp elyte langevin 300.0 300.0 100.0 12345

# --- Output ---
thermo 100
thermo_style custom step temp pe ke vol density f_fxconp

dump 1 all custom 100 traj.lammpstrj id type x y z q

# --- Run ---
minimize 1e-6 1e-9 1000 10000
run 10000











Issue
Cause
Solution




Charge oscillates wildly
eta too small or too large
Try eta = 1.0 or 2.0 (real units)


Matrix inversion fails
Singular matrix
Increase eta or check geometry


NaN in output
Overlapping atoms
Minimize before dynamics


Slow performance
Large matrix storage
Use algo mat_cg or algo cg


kspace style not supported
Wrong kspace for ELECTRODE
Use pppm/electrode

title: Electrostatics
text:
TipIn this section




Why long-range Coulomb is computationally hard
How Ewald summation splits the problem
How PPPM achieves O(N log N) scaling
Why slab geometry needs special treatment
Pair-kpace consistency rules





Electrostatic interactions are long-range:
\[V(r) = k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r}\]
Unlike LJ (which decays as r⁻⁶), Coulomb falls off slowly. In a periodic system, the sum of all pairwise Coulomb interactions does not converge quickly — you cannot simply cut it off at a reasonable distance without introducing large errors.



Direct summation
Cost
Problem




All pairs (N²/2)
O(N²)
Prohibitive for large N


Cutoff at 10 Å
O(N)
~10% error for ionic systems



The challenge: we need the long-range part of Coulomb for accuracy, but we cannot sum it directly because there are too many pairs.





Ewald summation splits the Coulomb sum into three parts:
\[V_{Coul} = V_{real} + V_{recip} + V_{self}\]








Term
Description
How It’s Computed




Real space
Short-range Coulomb (direct sum)
Cutoff-based; fast for small r


Reciprocal space
Long-range (Fourier transform)
FFT-based; fast for large N


Self term
Corrects for double-counting
Analytic formula







Smear each charge into a Gaussian cloud (width determined by α)
Real space: interaction of Gaussians with original charges (short-range, convergent)
Reciprocal space: interaction of Gaussians with each other in Fourier space (long-range, also convergent)
Self term: subtract the interaction of each charge with its own Gaussian




α controls the width of the Gaussian smearing:



α (large)
α (small)




Narrow Gaussians
Wide Gaussians


Real space converges quickly
Real space converges slowly


Reciprocal space expensive
Reciprocal space cheaper


Overall: fast for small systems
Overall: better for large systems



Typical α ≈ 0.2–0.5 Å⁻¹ (real units). LAMMPS usually chooses a reasonable default, but for very asymmetric boxes (very thin in one direction), tuning helps.



kspace_style ewald 1e-5
1e-5 = desired RMS force accuracy (relative to force magnitude). Tighter tolerance = more accurate = slower.






Ewald scales as O(N³/²). For very large systems, this is still prohibitive.
PPPM (also called PME — Particle Mesh Ewald) maps charges to a regular mesh and uses FFT for the reciprocal space sum:
\[O(N \log N) \text{ scaling}\]




Distribute charges to mesh: each charge assigned to nearby mesh points (Gaussian or cloud-in-cell)
FFT to reciprocal space: charge density(r) → charge density(k)
Multiply by Green’s function: apply the Coulomb kernel in k-space
FFT back to real space: forces on mesh
Interpolate forces to particles: mesh forces → atomic forces

The key advantage: FFT is O(N log N), so the reciprocal space part scales much better than Ewald.



kspace_style pppm 1e-5

Speed

Standard

For production: 1e-5 is usually sufficient. For precise energy calculations: 1e-6.

kspace_style none                   # explicitly no long-range
DO NOT use for charged systems or electrolytes. The long-range part is significant — cutting it off introduces errors of 10–50%.




Neutral, sparse systems (gases)
Very short simulations where speed matters more than accuracy
Testing/debugging before production




For small systems (N < 1000) with short simulation times (ns), cutoff-based may be acceptable. For anything involving ions, water, or electrode interfaces: use PPPM.






With boundary p p p, the system is a periodic tile. Ewald/PPPM works straightforwardly.



For electrode-electrolyte simulations:
boundary p p f    # non-periodic z
The z-direction has a vacuum gap. This creates two electrode surfaces exposed to vacuum (or vacuum above the electrolyte).
Problem with slab geometry: electrostatics in 2D is different from 3D. The naive Ewald/PPPM sum would include artificial dipole-dipole interactions between periodic images in z.
Solution: 2D Ewald / slab correction
kspace_modify slab 3
This applies a correction for the slab geometry: - Assumes the system is infinitely periodic in x, y - Assumes finite (non-periodic) in z - Adds a dipole correction term






WarningForgot kspace_modify slab?



If you use boundary p p f without kspace_modify slab, you will get: - Artificially high pressure in z-direction - Incorrect forces on atoms near the surface - Wrong double-layer structure
Always add kspace_modify slab N for non-periodic z.





boundary p p p    # fully periodic
# In fix electrode/conp:
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 couple top 1.0 ffield on
With ffield on, the system is treated as an infinite stack of identical cells: - No vacuum region - Smaller z-dimension possible (saves atoms) - Requires symm on (total charge neutrality) - Uses internal E-field to apply potential difference

title: Force Fields
text:
What Is a Force Field?
A force field is a set of mathematical functions and parameters that describe interatomic forces. It is an approximation — no force field is “correct”, only more or less appropriate for a given system.
The components of a force field:



Component
What It Describes
Typical Functional Form




Non-bonded
Van der Waals, electrostatics
LJ, Coulomb


Bonded
Chemical bonds
Harmonic, Morse


Angle
Three-body bending
Harmonic, cosine


Dihedral
Four-body torsion
Trigonometric series

title: Force Fields
text:
Non-Bonded Interactions

Van der Waals (Dispersion/Repulsion)
The Lennard-Jones (LJ) potential is the most common:
\[V(r) = 4\epsilon \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} - \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^6 \right]\]








Parameter
Physical Meaning
Typical Values (real units)




\(\epsilon\)
Depth of energy well (binding strength)
0.1–0.2 kcal/mol for atoms


\(\sigma\)
Distance where energy = zero
3.0–4.0 Å for light atoms



Term-by-term breakdown:

r⁻¹² term: Steep repulsion at short range (Pauli exclusion)
r⁻⁶ term: Softer attraction at longer range (London dispersion)

Visual representation:








Figure 1: Lennard-Jones potential: repulsion at short range, attraction at longer range





The minimum of the LJ potential is at \(r_{min} = 2^{1/6}\sigma \approx 1.12\sigma\).

LJ in LAMMPS
pair_style lj/cut 10.0    # LJ with cutoff at 10 Å
pair_coeff 1 1 0.15 3.5   # type 1-type 1: epsilon=0.15, sigma=3.5
pair_coeff 1 2 0.10 3.3   # type 1-type 2: mixed values
Cutoff considerations: - LJ is truncated at rcut — introduces error - Typical rcut = 10–12 Å for water - Energy drift indicates cutoff too small - Never exceed half the minimum box dimension



Coulombic Electrostatics
\[V(r) = k \frac{q_1 q_2}{r}\]
Long-range and never truly zero. This is why special methods (Ewald, PPPM) are needed — see ?@sec-electrostatics.
In LAMMPS:
pair_style lj/cut/coul/long 10.0   # LJ + real-space Coulomb; k-space handles long-range
pair_coeff * * 0.15 3.5            # LJ parameters for all pairs
pair_coeff 1 1 0.0 0.0             # no LJ for some pairs
kspace_style pppm 1e-5             # long-range solver


Combined Short-Range Potentials
pair_style lj/cut/coul/long 10.0    # Most common for electrolyte simulations
pair_style born/coul/long 10.0       # For ionic crystals with repulsion term
pair_style 12-6-4/long               # For metal oxides (adds 1/r⁴ term)
The pair style MUST be compatible with the kspace style:








Pair Style
Kspace Style
Notes




lj/cut/coul/long
pppm or ewald
Standard for electrolytes


lj/cut/coul/cut
none
Direct Coulomb only; error if cutoff too small


coul/long only
pppm
No LJ; pure Coulomb





Bonded Interactions

Bonds
Harmonic bond (most common):
\[V(r) = k (r - r_0)^2\]
bond_style harmonic
bond_coeff 1 300 1.0    # k=300 kcal/mol/Å², r0=1.0 Å


Angles
Harmonic angle:
\[V(\theta) = k (\theta - \theta_0)^2\]
angle_style harmonic
angle_coeff 1 40 109.5    # k=40 kcal/mol/rad², theta0=109.5°


Dihedrals
Proper dihedral (trigonometric series):
\[V(\phi) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} k_n \cos(n\phi - \phi_n)\]
dihedral_style opls              # OPLS-style dihedrals
dihedral_coeff 1 0.5 0.0 3 0.0  # k, n, phi0 parameters






NoteWhen Bonded Interactions Matter




Water models (TIP3P, TIP4P): explicit O-H bonds and H-O-H angle
Organic molecules: bonds, angles, dihedrals all needed
Simple electrolytes (NaCl in water): no bonds; only non-bonded interactions
Ionic crystals: bonds may be implicit (pair_style only)

When in doubt: check your water model’s structure. If it has bond_style and angle_style, you need those coefficients.

When two different atom types interact, we need parameters for the cross-pair.

Lorentz-Berthelot Mixing
pair_coeff 1 1 epsilon1 sigma1    # type 1 - type 1
pair_coeff 2 2 epsilon2 sigma2    # type 2 - type 2
# type 1 - type 2 is computed as:
epsilon_12 = sqrt(epsilon1 * epsilon2)
sigma_12 = (sigma1 + sigma2) / 2


Explicit Cross-Parameters
pair_coeff 1 2 epsilon12 sigma12    # override mixing rule
For electrolyte-electrode interactions: explicit cross-parameters are often better than mixing rules.

title: Constant Potential Molecular Dynamics in LAMMPS — Learning Taxonomy
text:
Introductory mechanics and electromagnetism (Coulomb’s law, electrostatic energy)
Basic chemistry (ions, water structure, what an electrode is)
One programming language (any) — for post-processing
No prior MD experience required





You have LAMMPS installed (or access to an HPC cluster with it)
You can run an input script and see log output
You want to understand what the commands mean, not just what they do





The goal is to connect LAMMPS input lines → physical meaning → simulation output
Theory sections explain the physics; Implementation sections show the corresponding LAMMPS syntax
Every major concept links to an observable you can measure









Newton determines atomic motion; forces come from interatomic potentials
A timestep Δt advances positions and velocities: x(t+Δt) = x(t) + v(t)Δt
Forces are recalculated at every step — this is what makes MD computationally expensive
The trajectory is a deterministic sequence; statistics over many steps give thermodynamic properties





Units — define the physical scale (real = Å, kcal/mol, fs; metal = Å, eV, ps). Mismatch causes garbage.
Atom style — what properties each particle carries. charge is mandatory for electrostatics.
Boundary — p p f means periodic in x,y, fixed (non-periodic) in z. Determines slab geometry for electrode simulations.
Pair styles — the functional form of the interatomic potential. Determines what forces exist.
Fixes — operations applied every timestep (integration, thermostats, constraints). The verb of LAMMPS.
Computes — calculate quantities on the fly (temperature, stress, charge density)
Groups — named subsets of atoms for targeted commands. Essential for distinguishing electrode from electrolyte.





Thermodynamic output — energy (total, kinetic, potential), temperature, pressure, volume
Energy conservation indicates a well-behaved simulation (NVE without thermostat)
Potential energy components (pair, bond, kspace) reveal where computation time goes
Drift in conserved quantity signals integration problems









A force field is a set of mathematical functions that describe interatomic forces
It is an approximation — no force field is “correct”, only appropriate for certain systems
Choice of force field determines what physics is captured (and what is omitted)
All force field parameters are fitted to experimental data or quantum calculations







Lennard-Jones (LJ): pair_style lj/cut — the workhorse of MD

Formula: V(r) = 4ε[(σ/r)^12 - (σ/r)^6]
ε = depth of the energy well (binding strength); σ = distance at which energy = zero
The r⁻¹² term is steep repulsion at short range; r⁻⁶ is softer attraction at longer range
Physical meaning: Pauli repulsion at short distance, induced-dipole attraction at longer range
Cutoff: LJ is truncated at some rcut — introduces error; rcut typically 10–12 Å for water
Why cut? Computation scales as N²; truncation saves time with acceptable error

Other forms: Buckingham, Morse, 12-6-4 (for metals), Gaussian — each suited to different materials





Formula: V(r) = k q₁q₂/r — long-range, never truly zero
The problem: Direct summation scales as N²; prohibitive for large systems
Solutions: Ewald summation, PPPM (Particle-Particle Particle-Mesh) — see Section 3





pair_style lj/cut/coul/long — LJ plus real-space Coulomb; k-space handles the long-range Coulomb
This is the standard choice for electrolyte simulations: LJ for repulsion/attraction, Coulomb for ionic interactions






Bonds: bond_style harmonic — spring-like; V = k(r - r₀)²

Water models (TIP3P, TIP4P) have explicit O-H bonds
Electrolyte ions may have internal bonds (e.g., carbonate)

Angles: angle between three atoms; important for water orientation
Dihedrals: rotations around bonds; relevant for organic electrolytes





Mixing rules: Lorentz-Berthelot (ε_ij = √(ε_i ε_j), σ_ij = (σ_i + σ_j)/2)
pair_coeff syntax: ID1 ID2 epsilon sigma for each unique pair type
All pairs must be defined: LAMMPS will error if any pair type is unspecified





Water models: TIP3P, TIP4P, SPC/E — each is a compromise between accuracy and cost
Ion parameters: from literature (e.g., Joung & Cheatham, 2008)
Electrode atoms: typically large ε for hard-wall repulsion, no Coulomb (metallic screening)
Physical meaning of LJ on electrodes: prevents electrolyte atoms from penetrating the surface; does not model bonding











Input
Output Effect

Potential energy scale; particle density; diffusion coefficient


dielectric
Strength of Coulomb interactions (vacuum = 1, water ≈ 80)


bond_style + bond_coeff
Vibrational spectra; bulk modulus; compressibility


Cutoff distance
Energy drift; simulation runtime (larger cut = slower but more accurate)











Real experiments control T, P (or V), and composition
In MD, we control what we simulate: NVE (microcanonical), NVT (canonical), NPT (isothermal-isobaric)
The choice is not just convention — it determines which statistical ensemble produces your output







Position update: x(t+Δt) = 2x(t) - x(t-Δt) + (F/m)Δt² (Verlet integration)
Velocity Verlet: v(t) = v(t-Δt) + 0.5(F(t) + F(t+Δt))Δt — more stable
Δt must be small enough to resolve the fastest motion (typically C-H bond vibration)
Typical values: Δt = 1 fs for explicit water; Δt = 0.5 fs if bonds are flexible; Δt = 2 fs with bond constraints





Too large Δt → energy drift, simulation “blows up” (atoms overlap catastrophically)
Too small Δt → wasted computation; results unchanged
Constraint: fix shake or fix rattle removes fast degrees of freedom, allowing larger Δt

fix 1 all nvt          # NVE + thermostat (see below)

nve = no thermostat; energy should be conserved (check E_total drift in log)
nvt = NVE modified by thermostat; total energy is NOT conserved








Temperature is a statistical property: T = (2/3Nk) × (1/2 mv²)_avg
Instantaneous T fluctuates; we average over time to compare to experiment
Thermostats manipulate velocities to sample the canonical ensemble

Too high T → bond breaking, chemical reactions (LAMMPS not suited for this)
Too low T → slow dynamics, metastable states

Mechanical pressure from forces + kinetic contribution

Coulomb: V ∝ 1/r — long-range even at moderate distances
Direct summation: N(N-1)/2 pairs → computationally prohibitive for N > 1000
Periodic boundaries make the math non-trivial (Ewald, slab corrections)







Real space: short-range Coulomb interactions summed directly (cutoff-based)
Reciprocal space: long-range interactions handled via Fourier transform
Self term: corrects for double-counting of interactions in periodic systems





Controls the split between real and reciprocal space
Large α → narrow real-space Gaussian → faster real-space convergence → slower k-space
Small α → opposite
LAMMPS default is usually reasonable; for charged systems with small box, tuning may help








Ewald: O(N³/²) scaling — still bad for very large N
PPPM: maps charge to mesh, uses FFT → O(N log N)
Standard for systems with >10,000 atoms




kspace_style pppm 1e-5

1e-5 = desired RMS force accuracy (relative to force magnitude)
Tighter tolerance = more accurate but slower
For electrode systems: kspace_style pppm/electrode 1e-5






Small systems (N < 1000) or very short simulations: direct Coulomb with cutoff may suffice
pair_style coul/cut 10.0 — cutoff at 10 Å; no k-space calculation
Warning: ignoring long-range electrostatics introduces serious error; do not use for production







boundary p p f — z is non-periodic
Electrostatics requires 2D Ewald correction: kspace_modify slab 3
Without this, forces in z-direction are wrong (artificial dipole-dipole interactions)





boundary p p p with ffield yes in ELECTRODE fix
Internal E-field applied; simulates infinite stack of identical cells
No slab correction needed; better for some geometries






pair_style lj/cut/coul/long MUST pair with kspace_style pppm (or ewald)
pair_style lj/cut/coul/cut pairs with NO kspace (direct Coulomb only)
Mismatch causes LAMMPS to error or produce wrong forces









Insulator: charges are fixed; electrostatic potential varies freely
Conductor: charges redistribute to equalize potential within the material
Electrode (metal): behaves as conductor; charges respond to applied voltage







AMBER, CHARMM, OPLS — atomic charges set at start, never change
Appropriate for insulators and vacuum
Problem for electrodes: charge cannot respond to applied potential





Drude oscillators: extra particle attached by harmonic spring; models electron cloud response
Core-shell: massless shell encloses ion; responds to local field
QEq (charge equilibration): redistribute charges within a single molecule
CPM (Constant Potential Method): controls boundary condition on electrostatic potential








Ions accumulate near charged surfaces → electric double layer
Water molecules orient near electrode (hydrogen up/down)
Capacitance depends on ion size, hydration, electrode structure





Real experiments: potentiostat holds electrode at fixed voltage
Fixed-charge MD: cannot enforce voltage; can only set atom charges (wrong)
CPM: enforces voltage directly → correct electrochemical interface








We want: electrostatic potential on electrode surface = V (fixed)
We have: electrode charges, electrolyte charges, geometry
Energy: E = (1/2) Σ q_i φ_i — depends on all charges
Constraint: electrode potentials must equal specified values





Minimize E(q) subject to Aq = V (potential constraints)
Solution: induced surface charges that depend on geometry and electrolyte
These are NOT predetermined — they emerge from the minimization





Point charges at surface → singular matrix (diverges as r → 0)
Smear each charge as a Gaussian distribution (width η)
η controls smearing: larger η = narrower (more point-like); smaller η = wider
Physical meaning: metals have finite electron density at surface; smearing mimics this





N×N matrix relates electrode potentials to charges:
Q = Q₀ᵥ + C · V
Q₀ᵥ = charge at zero applied potential (influenced by electrolyte structure)
C = capacitance matrix (depends on electrode geometry and dielectric)
Physical meaning: Cij = how much charge on electrode i changes when electrode j’s potential changes

Newton determines atomic motion; forces come from interatomic potentials
A timestep Δt advances positions and velocities: x(t+Δt) = x(t) + v(t)Δt
Forces are recalculated at every step — this is what makes MD computationally expensive
The trajectory is a deterministic sequence; statistics over many steps give thermodynamic properties

Boundary — p p f means periodic in x,y, fixed (non-periodic) in z. Determines slab geometry for electrode simulations.
Pair styles — the functional form of the interatomic potential. Determines what forces exist.
Fixes — operations applied every timestep (integration, thermostats, constraints). The verb of LAMMPS.
Computes — calculate quantities on the fly (temperature, stress, charge density)
Groups — named subsets of atoms for targeted commands. Essential for distinguishing electrode from electrolyte.

text:
A force field is a set of mathematical functions that describe interatomic forces
It is an approximation — no force field is “correct”, only appropriate for certain systems
Choice of force field determines what physics is captured (and what is omitted)
All force field parameters are fitted to experimental data or quantum calculations







Lennard-Jones (LJ): pair_style lj/cut — the workhorse of MD

Formula: V(r) = 4ε[(σ/r)^12 - (σ/r)^6]
ε = depth of the energy well (binding strength); σ = distance at which energy = zero
The r⁻¹² term is steep repulsion at short range; r⁻⁶ is softer attraction at longer range
Physical meaning: Pauli repulsion at short distance, induced-dipole attraction at longer range
Cutoff: LJ is truncated at some rcut — introduces error; rcut typically 10–12 Å for water
Why cut? Computation scales as N²; truncation saves time with acceptable error

Other forms: Buckingham, Morse, 12-6-4 (for metals), Gaussian — each suited to different materials





Formula: V(r) = k q₁q₂/r — long-range, never truly zero
The problem: Direct summation scales as N²; prohibitive for large systems
Solutions: Ewald summation, PPPM (Particle-Particle Particle-Mesh) — see Section 3





pair_style lj/cut/coul/long — LJ plus real-space Coulomb; k-space handles the long-range Coulomb
This is the standard choice for electrolyte simulations: LJ for repulsion/attraction, Coulomb for ionic interactions






Bonds: bond_style harmonic — spring-like; V = k(r - r₀)²

Water models (TIP3P, TIP4P) have explicit O-H bonds
Electrolyte ions may have internal bonds (e.g., carbonate)

Angles: angle between three atoms; important for water orientation
Dihedrals: rotations around bonds; relevant for organic electrolytes





Mixing rules: Lorentz-Berthelot (ε_ij = √(ε_i ε_j), σ_ij = (σ_i + σ_j)/2)
pair_coeff syntax: ID1 ID2 epsilon sigma for each unique pair type
All pairs must be defined: LAMMPS will error if any pair type is unspecified

Ion parameters: from literature (e.g., Joung & Cheatham, 2008)
Electrode atoms: typically large ε for hard-wall repulsion, no Coulomb (metallic screening)
Physical meaning of LJ on electrodes: prevents electrolyte atoms from penetrating the surface; does not model bonding

Real experiments control T, P (or V), and composition
In MD, we control what we simulate: NVE (microcanonical), NVT (canonical), NPT (isothermal-isobaric)
The choice is not just convention — it determines which statistical ensemble produces your output







Position update: x(t+Δt) = 2x(t) - x(t-Δt) + (F/m)Δt² (Verlet integration)
Velocity Verlet: v(t) = v(t-Δt) + 0.5(F(t) + F(t+Δt))Δt — more stable
Δt must be small enough to resolve the fastest motion (typically C-H bond vibration)
Typical values: Δt = 1 fs for explicit water; Δt = 0.5 fs if bonds are flexible; Δt = 2 fs with bond constraints





Too large Δt → energy drift, simulation “blows up” (atoms overlap catastrophically)
Too small Δt → wasted computation; results unchanged
Constraint: fix shake or fix rattle removes fast degrees of freedom, allowing larger Δt

Instantaneous T fluctuates; we average over time to compare to experiment

text:
Coulomb: V ∝ 1/r — long-range even at moderate distances
Direct summation: N(N-1)/2 pairs → computationally prohibitive for N > 1000
Periodic boundaries make the math non-trivial (Ewald, slab corrections)







Real space: short-range Coulomb interactions summed directly (cutoff-based)
Reciprocal space: long-range interactions handled via Fourier transform
Self term: corrects for double-counting of interactions in periodic systems





Controls the split between real and reciprocal space
Large α → narrow real-space Gaussian → faster real-space convergence → slower k-space
Small α → opposite
LAMMPS default is usually reasonable; for charged systems with small box, tuning may help








Ewald: O(N³/²) scaling — still bad for very large N
PPPM: maps charge to mesh, uses FFT → O(N log N)
Standard for systems with >10,000 atoms




kspace_style pppm 1e-5

1e-5 = desired RMS force accuracy (relative to force magnitude)
Tighter tolerance = more accurate but slower

text:
Insulator: charges are fixed; electrostatic potential varies freely
Conductor: charges redistribute to equalize potential within the material
Electrode (metal): behaves as conductor; charges respond to applied voltage







AMBER, CHARMM, OPLS — atomic charges set at start, never change
Appropriate for insulators and vacuum
Problem for electrodes: charge cannot respond to applied potential





Drude oscillators: extra particle attached by harmonic spring; models electron cloud response
Core-shell: massless shell encloses ion; responds to local field
QEq (charge equilibration): redistribute charges within a single molecule
CPM (Constant Potential Method): controls boundary condition on electrostatic potential








Ions accumulate near charged surfaces → electric double layer
Water molecules orient near electrode (hydrogen up/down)
Capacitance depends on ion size, hydration, electrode structure





Real experiments: potentiostat holds electrode at fixed voltage
Fixed-charge MD: cannot enforce voltage; can only set atom charges (wrong)
CPM: enforces voltage directly → correct electrochemical interface








We want: electrostatic potential on electrode surface = V (fixed)
We have: electrode charges, electrolyte charges, geometry
Energy: E = (1/2) Σ q_i φ_i — depends on all charges
Constraint: electrode potentials must equal specified values





Minimize E(q) subject to Aq = V (potential constraints)
Solution: induced surface charges that depend on geometry and electrolyte
These are NOT predetermined — they emerge from the minimization





Point charges at surface → singular matrix (diverges as r → 0)
Smear each charge as a Gaussian distribution (width η)
η controls smearing: larger η = narrower (more point-like); smaller η = wider
Physical meaning: metals have finite electron density at surface; smearing mimics this





N×N matrix relates electrode potentials to charges:
Q = Q₀ᵥ + C · V
Q₀ᵥ = charge at zero applied potential (influenced by electrolyte structure)
C = capacitance matrix (depends on electrode geometry and dielectric)
Physical meaning: Cij = how much charge on electrode i changes when electrode j’s potential changes

title: Constant Potential Molecular Dynamics in LAMMPS
text:
Prerequisites
This guide assumes you have:

Completed introductory physics (mechanics, electromagnetism basics)
Completed one semester of general chemistry (ions, Coulomb’s law)
Basic programming experience (any language)
Access to a LAMMPS installation (binary or source; CMake-built with ELECTRODE and KSPACE packages)

No prior MD experience is required.

title: Constant Potential Molecular Dynamics in LAMMPS

Computing Environment
All examples in this guide assume a standard LAMMPS installation. Commands shown in code blocks like:
lmp -in in.electrode -pk gpu 1 -l yes
should be run in a terminal where LAMMPS is available.

TipIn this section




What NVE, NVT, NPT mean and when to use each
How thermostats work (algorithms, LAMMPS syntax, physical meaning)
How barostats control pressure and volume
Timestep selection and why it matters
What observables you can measure





Real experiments control temperature, pressure, and composition. In MD, we choose which of these to hold fixed — this determines the statistical ensemble and thus which thermodynamic properties we can legitimately compute.

The ensemble choice is not just convention — it determines which statistical mechanics formula you must use to connect simulation results to experimental observables.





MD integrates Newton’s equations numerically. The velocity Verlet algorithm:
# Velocity Verlet (per atom)
v(t + dt/2) = v(t) + 0.5 * F(t) / m * dt        # half-step velocity
x(t + dt) = x(t) + v(t + dt/2) * dt             # full-step position
F(t + dt) = forces(x(t + dt))                  # new forces
v(t + dt) = v(t + dt/2) + 0.5 * F(t + dt) / m * dt  # complete velocity



The timestep Δt must be small enough to resolve the fastest motion in the system:



Motion
Characteristic Frequency
Δt Limit

requires small Δt

Typical values:

1 fs for explicit water with flexible bonds
0.5 fs for flexible molecules with H-bonds
2 fs with bond constraints (fix shake or fix rattle)

Energy drift; simulation “blows up”
Wasted computation

Diminishing returns



Validation: Run NVE and check energy conservation. Acceptable drift: < 0.1% of total energy over 1 ns.



fix shake or fix rattle removes fast degrees of freedom (C-H, O-H bonds) by constraint:
fix constrain all shake 1e-4 200 0 a 1.0    # constrain bond with tolerance 1e-4
Allows Δt = 2 fs (2× faster simulation, same accuracy for bonded motion).






Temperature is a statistical property, not a direct control variable:
\[T = \frac{2}{3Nk_B} \left\langle \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \right\rangle\]
The instantaneous temperature fluctuates. Thermostats manipulate atom velocities to sample the canonical ensemble correctly.





fix tempctr all temp/rescale 10 300.0 300.0 0.02 1.0
Simple scaling: multiply all velocities to match target T. Not rigorous — does not produce correct fluctuations. Useful for quick equilibration.



fix ber all berendsen temp 300.0 300.0 100.0
Weak coupling to heat bath. Produces incorrect fluctuations (variance too low). Not recommended for production.



fix nvt_all all nvt temp 300.0 300.0 100.0
Extended system method. The system + thermostat share energy. Produces correct canonical distribution. Standard for most production runs.
Variants: - fix nvt/kk — Kokkos version for GPU - fix nvt/sphere — for angular degrees of freedom



fix mylang all langevin 300.0 300.0 100.0 12345
Stochastic differential equation:
\[m\frac{dv}{dt} = F - \gamma mv + \sqrt{2\gamma m k_B T} \, \xi(t)\]

Physical Meaning

Conservative force

Damping (friction)


√(2γmk_BT) ξ(t)
Random noise (thermal fluctuations)



Good for: - Non-equilibrium dynamics (shear, field) - Systems with heterogeneous dynamics - When you want explicit noise
Parameter choice: - 100.0 = damping time (fd). Too small = over-damped; too large = slow equipartition - 12345 = random seed (set explicitly for reproducibility)

The mechanical pressure is computed from atomic forces and positions. For anisotropic systems (slabs), the pressure tensor has different components.





fix npt_all all npt temp 300.0 300.0 100.0 iso 1.0 1.0 500.0
Controls T (Nosé-Hoover) and P (Nosé-Hoover). The iso keyword applies isotropic pressure control.
Keywords: - iso — isotropic (all components same P) - aniso — anisotropic (x, y, z independently) - semiiso — semi-isotropic (xy coupled, z separate)
For slab geometries with non-periodic z:
fix npt_xz all npt temp 300.0 300.0 100.0 semiiso 1.0 1.0 500.0
This controls P_x = P_y, but allows P_z to adjust independently (or vice versa depending on setup).

title: Electrodes and the Constant Potential Method
text:
TipIn this section




Why conductors need different treatment than insulators in MD
What the constant potential method does (and why it matters for electrochemistry)
How induced charges emerge from energy minimization
The capacitance matrix and what it tells you







In a typical molecular simulation (water, proteins, simple electrolytes):

Atomic charges are fixed at their initial values
The electrostatic potential within the material varies freely depending on charge distribution
No charge redistribution occurs during the simulation

This is appropriate for insulators, where charges cannot move through the material.



In a metal (electrode):

Charges (electrons) can move freely within the material
The material adjusts its charge distribution to equalize the electrostatic potential
This happens on timescales much faster than atomic motion (effectively instantaneous)

If we treat a metal electrode with fixed charges, we’re getting the physics wrong — the electrode cannot maintain arbitrary charge distributions.






When an electrode is placed in electrolyte:

Electric double layer: ions accumulate near the charged surface
Solvation shells: water molecules orient near the surface
Applied potential: changing the electrode voltage changes ion adsorption




In real electrochemistry, the potential (voltage) of the electrode is the controlled variable, measured and maintained by a potentiostat.
In a typical MD simulation with fixed atom charges, we can only control the total charge on the electrode — not the potential. This is wrong for electrochemistry.









Controlled Variable
Physical Reality
Fixed-Charge MD
Constant Potential




Electrode potential
What the potentiostat controls
❌ Cannot enforce
✅ Direct control


Electrode charge
Flows from potential
✅ Can set
❌ Fluctuates






Consider a simulation of charging a supercapacitor:

We start with neutral electrodes
We want to apply 1 V between electrodes
With fixed charges: we must choose some total charge on each electrode — but what charge gives 1 V?
The relationship between charge and potential depends on the electrolyte structure (which we don’t know a priori)

With constant potential, the charges emerge from the physics — we specify the voltage and the simulation determines the induced charge.






We have a system with: - Electrode atoms with unknown charges \(q_i\) - Electrolyte atoms with known charges \(Q_j\) - A constraint: each electrode surface must be at potential \(V\)
The electrostatic energy:
\[E(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{Q}) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} q_i \, A_{ij} \, q_j + \sum_{i,j} q_i \, A_{ij} \, Q_j + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} Q_i \, A_{ij} \, Q_j\]
Where \(A_{ij}\) is the inverse capacitance matrix (from the kspace solver).
We want to minimize \(E\) subject to the constraint that each electrode group is at potential \(V_k\).



Mathematically: - Minimize \(E(\mathbf{q})\) - Subject to \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}\) (the potential constraints)
The solution gives induced charges that depend on: - Electrode geometry - Electrolyte structure - Applied potential
These are NOT predetermined — they emerge from the minimization.





Point charges at the electrode surface create a singularity — as an electrolyte ion approaches the surface, the interaction energy diverges (Coulomb catastrophe). This makes the matrix ill-conditioned and difficult to invert.



Smear each electrode charge over a Gaussian distribution:
\[\rho_i(\mathbf{r}) = q_i \left(\frac{\eta_i}{\pi}\right)^{3/2} \exp(-\eta_i |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{R}_i|^2)\]
The smearing width η (eta) controls:







η (large)
η (small)




Narrow distribution (more like point charge)
Wide distribution (smoother, better conditioned)


More accurate electrostatics near surface
Better matrix convergence; smoother potential


Harder to converge (singular matrix)
Easier to solve



Typical η ≈ 1.0–2.0 Å⁻² (real units) or 0.2–0.5 (metal units).






NotePhysical Interpretation of Smearing



Smearing mimics the fact that real metals have a finite electron density at the surface — the charges are not point-like. The Gaussian width parameter should be chosen to match the electron gas density of the electrode material.






The N×N capacitance matrix \(\mathbf{C}\) relates electrode potentials to electrode charges:
\[\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{Q}_{0V} + \mathbf{C} \cdot \mathbf{V}\]







Symbol
Meaning




\(\mathbf{Q}\)
Total charge on each electrode group


\(\mathbf{Q}_{0V}\)
Charge configuration at zero applied potential (influenced by electrolyte)


\(\mathbf{C}\)
Capacitance matrix; depends only on geometry and dielectric


\(\mathbf{V}\)
Applied potentials on each electrode group



Physical meaning of C_ij: How much charge on electrode i changes when electrode j’s potential changes, with all other potentials held constant.
What you can compute from C: - Total capacitance: \(C_{total} = \sum_{i,j} C_{ij}\) - Differential capacitance: \(dQ/dV\) at given V - Potential distribution in complex geometries











Aspect
Constant Potential (electrode/conp)
Constant Charge (electrode/conq)




What is fixed
Voltage on each electrode group
Total charge on each electrode group


What fluctuates
Electrode atom charges
Electrode potentials


Physical analog
Potentiostat
Galvanostat


Use case
Electrochemical experiments
Battery discharge (known charge flux)


Output
Induced charges
Measured potentials





Constant potential (electrode/conp): - Comparing to electrochemical experiments - Studying double-layer structure at controlled voltage - Capacitance measurements
Constant charge (electrode/conq): - Modeling battery cycling (known current → known charge change) - When you know the amount of charge injected/extracted - Studying potential response to charging







The electric double layer has characteristic regions:

Inner layer (Helmholtz): specifically adsorbed ions, water molecules
Outer layer: solvated ions attracted by coulomb
Diffuse layer: decaying ion concentration into bulk

CPM captures all of these — ion density profiles near electrodes reflect the balance of electrostatic attraction and ionic excluded-volume effects.



Water molecules near electrodes: - Orient with H atoms toward negative electrode, O toward positive - Form layers (oscillating density) near the surface - This structure affects capacitance (Frumkin correction)
The force field (water model) determines how realistic this structure is.










Parameter
Effect on Capacitance




Ion size
Larger ions → lower capacitance (excluded volume)


Ion charge
Higher charge → stronger adsorption → different capacitance


Electrode structure
Sharp features (tips, edges) → field enhancement → higher local capacitance


Water model
Dielectric constant determines screening → affects capacitance


Temperature
Higher T → lower capacitance (thermal disruption of structure)










Voltage control: only CPM lets you specify the actual voltage (not just charge)
Induced charges: the correct charge distribution emerges from the physics
Complex geometries: for nanostructured electrodes, charge distribution is highly non-uniform — fixed charge models cannot capture this
Screening: electrolyte screening of electrode charges is properly accounted for












Method
What It Does
How CPM Differs




Drude oscillators
Adds extra particles for electronic polarizability
CPM controls boundary potential, not internal polarizability


Core-shell
Adds massless shell for ionic polarizability
CPM is for electrode boundaries


QEq (charge equilibration)
Redistributes charges within a single molecule
CPM handles electrode-electrolyte boundary


Fixed charge
No polarizability
Wrong for metals






CPM is a classical method. It does not compute electronic structure. For: - Accurate metal electronic response → use jellium models or DFT-based MD -QM/MM coupling → couple CPM to quantum region
The approximation in CPM: electrode charges respond instantly to electrostatic environment. This is reasonable for metals (electronic response is fast).
